newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq hopes for ties with U.S. after oil deal.
newsitem.headline: Iraq hopes for ties with U.S. after oil deal.

text.p: Iraq said on Thursday it hoped its acceptance this week of U.N. terms for an oil-for-food deal would persuade the U.S. administration to normalise ties with Baghdad.

"We hope after the implementation of the memorandum of understanding...the U.S. administration will realise that it would be better to conduct political talks with Iraq for the resumption of natural ties," Culture and Information Minister Hamed Youssef Hummadi said at a news conference.

However, he also attacked U.S. plans to evacuate from northern Iraq thousands of Kurds and others who might be at risk since Iraqi President Saddam Hussein sent troops into the Kurdish region in August.

Iraq on Monday accepted U.N. conditions to sell $2 billion of oil in a six-month period to buy food and medicine. The Security Council's sanctions committee on Wednesday accepted an oil pricing formula necessary for the deal to be implemented.
Hummadi said Iraq considered the deal "a transitory formula" on the path to having the six-year-old ban on its oil exports removed entirely.
Washington said this week 5,000 people -- employees of U.S.-linked non-governmental organisations and their families -- would be taken to neighbouring Turkey and eventually to the United States.
"The offering of an identity or legal status by the American administration to any Iraqi...in return of his or her cooperation with it for political ends...is a hostile act," Hummadi said.

About 2,100 aid workers working for the U.S. government were taken out in September, followed last month by 600 Iraqi opposition figures. Hummadi said the aid workers were used for "espionage purposes and to destabilise the government in Iraq."
Hummadi said Iraq was ready to restore ties with Arab Gulf states, including those that helped the U.S.-led military effort to eject its troops from Kuwait in 1991.

He said Iraq expected members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) "to reconsider their policy towards Iraq and seek the establishment of normal relations." The GCC groups Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Oman and the United Arab Emirates.
Kuwait, which Iraq invaded in 1990, shows no interest in rapprochement with its former occupier but the U.A.E. is asking Gulf states to turn a new page with Baghdad.
The ruling Baath party newspaper al-Thawra said on Thursday U.A.E.'s overtures were an expression of its "adherence to the values and principles of joint Arab action."
The United Nations clamped comprehensive trade sanctions on Iraq for the 1990 invasion. The oil-for-food deal is designed to alleviate the suffering of the Iraqi people because of the embargo.
"We look at this embargo as being a crime perpetrated by evil souls with despotic power, who want to murder a whole nation," Hummadi said.
